guard: the discovery document a real auth-service serves is accepted by the real consumer `cotal meshes add --from` validates it with; reverting the producer to the flat shape must be caught at the seam, not merely noticed by the producer's own fixtures
why: THE DEFECT THIS GUARDS was invisible to two panels because each side's tests build the shape
that side expects: the producer's smoke asserted the flat fields it had just written, and the
consumer's smoke fed itself a hand-written `userAuth` fixture. Nothing fed the server's actual
bytes to the consumer. So the only mutation worth running here is the one that puts the
producer back the way it was and asks whether the seam notices. A guard that cannot detect the
original bug is decoration.
AFTER-RESTORE REBUILD, and it is not tidiness. The suite starts the auth-service by
self-re-exec, and that child imports `@cotal-ai/auth` — i.e. dist, not the source the mutation
edits. Hence the build in `command`. mutation-proof restores SOURCE and not artifacts, so
without `afterRestore` a graded run would leave a local dist compiled FROM THE MUTANT: a
daemon serving the flat document again, with the source looking correct. dist is gitignored,
so git cannot be the recovery for it. Each mutation rebuilds after its own restore.
BOTH MUTATIONS WERE RE-AIMED after a first run graded them UNGRADABLE and WRONG-RED. Recording
why, because the corrections are the interesting part and a silent re-aim would hide them.
M1 originally deleted only the PRE-BIND wrapper line. That was self-contradictory: the bundle is
written twice (once before listen(), once after, because endpoints.url is only known post-bind),
so deleting the pre-bind line left the POST-BIND assignment still writing a correct wrapper. The
mutation applied, changed no served bytes, and the suite passed — which the tool correctly called
UNGRADABLE rather than SURVIVED, since a mutant that alters no behaviour proves nothing about
whether the suite reaches the file. The corrected mutation replaces the POST-BIND assignment
with `delete bundle.userAuth`; because both writes act on the same closure-shared object, that
delete also removes the key created by the PRE-BIND literal, so the served document is flat
without deleting both source statements.
M2's note was simply WRONG ON THE FACTS. It claimed a wrapper pinning the empty string would
still parse, so the kill would land on the pinned-URL cell. It does not parse: assertUserAuthInfo
drops an empty `endpoints.url` (mesh-registry.ts:140 spreads the url only when truthy) and
checkUserBundle then refuses at meshes-add.ts:278 with `pins no exchange endpoint`. So the empty
wrapper is caught AT THE SEAM, one cell earlier than predicted, and the suite exits before
reaching the pinned-URL assertion — exactly the WRONG-RED the tool reported. M2 now predicts the
seam cell, which is what the code actually does.
That the empty-URL case is refused by the consumer rather than by a bespoke check is worth
keeping: the two-phase construction hazard is real, and the shipped validator already closes it.
